name: Pastel de nata
description: Warm custard tart in shatter-crisp lard pastry, the top blistered almost black. Monks at Jerónimos sold them to survive after the 1834 dissolution; the Belém recipe is still secret. Eat standing, dusted with cinnamon, minutes out of the oven.

name: Bifana
description: Thin pork cutlets simmered in white wine, garlic and bay, piled into a soft papo-seco that soaks up the juice. Lisbon's version is wet and pale, not grilled like the Porto style. Mustard, a beer, eaten standing at the counter. Take napkins.

name: Pastéis de bacalhau
description: Croquettes of salt cod, potato and parsley, shaped between two spoons into a pointed rugby ball and fried till the ridges crisp. Cheap counter food since the 1800s, eaten warm or cold with a beer. The cheese-filled tourist version is modern.

name: Bacalhau à Brás
description: Shredded salt cod tangled with matchstick fries and onion, loosely bound in barely-set egg, black olives and parsley scattered over. Named for a 19th-century Bairro Alto tasqueiro. It should be creamy — if it's firm like an omelette, it sat too long.

name: Prego no pão
description: Garlicky beef steak slapped into a bread roll — traditionally the full stop to a seafood meal, ordered after the shellfish rather than instead of it. At the old cervejarias it arrives as dessert. Mustard and piri-piri; never well done.

name: Sardinhas assadas
description: Whole oily sardines charred over coals, fattest and best from June to August. During the Santo António festas the Alfama alleys fill with grills and smoke. Eat with your fingers off a slice of bread that catches the fat — then eat the bread.

name: Amêijoas à Bulhão Pato
description: Small clams steamed open in olive oil with unreasonable amounts of garlic, coriander and lemon. Named after a 19th-century poet who loved them. The broth is the point: use an empty shell as a scoop, then bread until the bowl is clean.

name: Arroz de marisco
description: Soupy tomato, coriander and shellfish rice brought to the table in its pot and ladled out wet, never fluffy. A coastal Sunday dish that became a restaurant set piece. Usually a two-person minimum and half an hour's cooking — order it first.

name: Polvo à lagareiro
description: Octopus boiled tender then roasted until the edges frizzle, drowned in olive oil — lagar is the olive press — with smashed potatoes and whole garlic cloves. Portugal eats more octopus per head than almost anywhere. The oil is the sauce.

name: Peixinhos da horta
description: Green beans in a light, blistered batter: 'little fish of the garden', invented as meat-free food for fast days. Portuguese missionaries carried the technique to Nagasaki, where it became tempura. Eat hot, with lemon, before the batter softens.

name: Bitoque
description: The everyday Portuguese lunch: a thin steak under a fried egg, with rice, fries and a wine-and-butter pan sauce. Break the yolk over the rice straight away — that is the sauce. Around €10 with wine, and the truest measure of any tasca.

name: Caracóis
description: Tiny snails simmered with garlic, oregano and piri-piri, served by the bowlful with cold beer. 'Há caracóis' chalked in a window means the season is open. Pull each one out with a toothpick, then drink the broth left in the bottom.

name: Iscas com elas
description: Pork liver marinated in wine, vinegar and garlic, then flashed in the pan — 'with them' meaning the boiled potatoes alongside. Lisbon tasca food from when offal was the cheap cut. Sour, iron-rich, strong. Order it where the tablecloths are paper.

name: Travesseiro de Sintra
description: A sugar-dusted puff-pastry 'pillow' filled with almond and egg cream, baked at Piriquita since 1862 and worth the train to Sintra. Eat one hot while the queue is still out the door, and carry a box of queijadas back down the hill.

name: Ginjinha
description: Sour-cherry liqueur, sweet and sticky, poured at standing-room counters since 1840. Ask for it 'com elas' and the boozy cherries come in the glass. A euro or so, one shot, drunk on the pavement — a pre-dinner ritual, not a dessert.
